title: Laetitia Mugerwa said women don't depreciate. She's right.
content:
## Women don't depreciate. They compound.

Laetitia Mugerwa said it cleaner than anyone else has: *"Women do not lose value over time. Instead, their experiences yield dividends that enhance their discernment, establish boundaries, and set standards they no longer feel the need to apologise for."*

Not a caption. An argument. The kind that lands because it names what we've been carrying without saying.

The piece—published on BellaNaija in April 2026—rejects the whole architecture. The one that treats women like phones with declining resale value. The one that whispers 23 is the peak and everything after is markdown. Mugerwa dismantles it in prose that doesn't apologize for being direct.

She's not asking for participation trophies. She's stating balance-sheet reality: experience isn't baggage. It's equity.

## Why diaspora women are screenshotting this

If you're reading this in London, Toronto, or Brooklyn, you know the weight is double.

You're fighting the objectification that affects all women. Plus the fetishization that comes with being African in predominantly white spaces. Plus the family WhatsApp group asking about your "plans" every December. Plus the aunties back home who started panicking when you turned 25 unmarried.

You've been building yourself into a full human. Switching careers, learning languages, traveling solo, making mistakes, getting back up. Each layer adds to who you are.

But somehow you're still expected to shrink. To apologize for taking up space. To pretend you haven't lived a full life before meeting "the one."

Mugerwa's essay is circulating through group chats with fire emojis and "periodt" reactions because it names the thing: we're done apologizing for being experienced.

The Ghanaian woman who speaks three languages and runs a fintech startup in Berlin isn't damaged goods because she's 32 and single. The Kenyan writer who's lived in four countries and published two books isn't "too much" because she has standards. The Nigerian engineer who bought her own flat in Manchester at 28 isn't intimidating—she's invested.

Mugerwa's voice cuts through the noise. Women aren't products with sell-by dates.

## The script is being rewritten everywhere

This conversation matters because African women are redrafting the timeline everywhere. Chimamanda's feminist declarations. Lupita's red carpet refusals to be modest. Your cousin who launched her beauty line in Nairobi and moved the family group chat from "when are you getting married" to "how's the Series A going."

We're watching a generation refuse reduction to relationship status or reproductive capacity. Women who've lived in three countries, speak four languages, and run companies aren't apologizing for being "too much" anymore.

Back home, the shift is visible. Young African women are choosing careers over early marriage. Traveling solo. Starting businesses. Buying their own homes. The old timeline—graduate, marry, procreate, disappear—is crumbling.

But the pushback is real. Traditional voices still murmur about women getting "too educated" or "too independent." Social media trolls still lecture about biological clocks and feminine submission.

Mugerwa's essay is the counter-argument, stated plainly: experience yields dividends.

## What we're building for the next generation

Every African woman reading this knows we're not just fighting for ourselves. We're fighting for our nieces, our goddaughters, our future daughters.

Imagine raising girls who never question their worth based on age or experience. Girls who see mistakes as lessons, not stains. Girls who set boundaries without explanation.

That's the world Mugerwa's words are scaffolding.

The beauty of her message is its economy. She's not asking for special treatment. She's stating fact: women grow more valuable with experience, not less. The same way a fund manager with twenty years of market cycles is worth more than a fresh graduate, not less.

Culture is currency. Perception shapes value. Mugerwa's essay shifts the perception.

## Where the conversation goes from here

This won't end with one viral essay. It's part of the larger continental shift—women reclaiming narrative, refusing others' timelines.

The group chats are buzzing. Sisters are forwarding screenshots to each other. Because sometimes you need someone else to say what you already know before you believe it's true.

Share Mugerwa's message with the women in your life who need to hear it. The ones questioning their worth because they're single at 30. The ones apologizing for having standards. The ones shrinking to fit boxes that were never designed for their full scale.

Her words are the reminder: You don't depreciate. You appreciate.

Your experiences aren't baggage. They're dividends. And the balance sheet doesn't lie.
